title.narrative: Assessing the Impact of War on Sudan Living Heritage

description.narrative:
Sudan boasts a rich tapestry of cultural diversity and a storied history, standing atop one of the world's oldest civilizations. Its strategic location in northeastern Africa has historically made it a crossroads for interactions among sub-Saharan, Central African, Mediterranean, and Arab cultures. This interplay between diverse cultures, including indigenous Sudanese ones, has endowed the nation with a distinctive array of intangible cultural heritage (ICH). This ICH not only enriches Sudan's cultural fabric but also contributes significantly to its historical narrative, fostering a sense of identity among its people. Moreover, the intangible cultural heritage of Sudan is not confined to the realm of aesthetics and traditions. It plays an instrumental role in enhancing the well-being of communities and various societal groups. These cultural practices promote social cohesion, strengthen bonds among community members, and provide a framework for passing down essential knowledge and skills. They are a source of resilience, offering valuable insights into sustainable practices that have allowed communities to thrive in diverse and often challenging environments.
As Sudan continues to evolve and adapt to contemporary changes, safeguarding and celebrating its intangible cultural heritage remain paramount. Preserving this living heritage ensures that future generations will have the opportunity to explore the multifaceted legacy of Sudan's past and its enduring impact on the nation's cultural identity and communal well-being.
Since 15 April 2023, when armed conflict erupted between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), the situation has rapidly deteriorated. The most severe impact has been felt in Khartoum, including Omdurman, Khartoum North, as well as Darfur, Kordofan, and the Blue Nile state.
This conflict has forced a significant portion of the population to abandon their homes due to the grave risks of violence, abduction, physical and sexual abuse, and property theft. As of November 2023, nearly 6.2 million people have been forced from their homes according to UN OCHA. Many have sought refuge in camps or settlements in regions where the conflict's effects are less severe, including Damazine, Sennar, Kosti, Gadarif, Kassala, Port Sudan, Halfa, Dongola, Atbara, and Shendi.
More than 1.1 million people of the total number of displaced have sought safety beyond Sudan's borders, in neighboring countries like Chad, the Central African Republic, Egypt, Ethiopia, and South Sudan, providing sanctuary for those escaping the turmoil. This crisis underscores the urgent need for swift engagement to ensure that the living heritage of these displaced communities is not another casualty of this conflict.
The consequences of the war on the intangible cultural heritage of Sudan have caused enormous damage, destruction, disruption, and distortion to the intangible cultural heritage of various communities in the country. Initial accounts provided by activists and on social media networks have indicated: • The demise (due to the complete collapse of the healthcare system), murder, severe injuring, long detention, and abuse of many intangible cultural heritage bearers and practitioners, including elderly bearers. • Loss of livelihoods and impoverishment of living heritage bearers. Practitioners such as traditional artists, craftspeople, and performers have lost their sources of livelihood due to the war. The burning and looting of popular markets deprived people of their income, and in turn led to the lack of raw materials and demand for crafts and other objects related to rituals and certain cultural practices. • Local communities, bearers, and experts of intangible cultural heritage have fled their homes, and offices, leaving behind valuable manuscripts, documentation, research, and other objects related to the safeguarding of intangible cultural heritage. • The dispersion of local communities, families, and groups, and their displacement to inhospitable environments and places, such as refugee camps, have severely affected the channels and contexts necessary for the transmission of traditional knowledge to younger generations. • The displacement of youth from their villages and shutting down of schools affected the practice of many forms of living heritage and the formal transmission and exchange of this living heritage. • The destruction and closure of all cultural spaces and entertainment venues in Khartoum State, where many traditional celebrations crucial to the social cohesion and wellbeing of communities have ceased. • The discontinuation of traditions and practices designed to resolve conflicts disrupts the potential pathways to peace inherent in the living heritage of communities. The jeopardy faced by this living heritage diminishes the ability of communities to actively engage as integral participants in the pursuit of enduring peace for Sudan.
Many priceless cultural assets that play a role in the practice, safeguarding, and transmission of living heritage are at direct risk from the war. These include recordings, historical photos of the Ministry of Culture collection, tapes and videos stored in the archives of the Omdurman Radio and Sudan TV, the archives of the Institute of African and Asian Studies, libraries of the University of Khartoum and other universities, the National Council of Cultural Heritage, the House of Heritage, as well as the collections of the Ethnographic Museum, Sudan National Museum, Palace Museum, Military Museum, and Khalifa House Museum. This also includes government documents, reports, manuscripts, deeds of land ownership, and religious manuscripts in Kordofan, Blue Nile, and Darfur States.
The Rationale of this project is to assess and address the impact of the ongoing war, as well as the impact of conflicts between the politically motivated indigenous groups, intercommunal violence, and the attacks of tribal militants in Khartoum Darfur, Blue Nile and the Southern Kordofan regions. Moreover, the whole situation is aggravated by the compounding effects of disasters caused by natural and human-induced hazards. These threats have a serious impact on the transmission and viability of the intangible cultural heritage of the 200 indigenous communities spread over all 18 states where 67 distinct languages are spoken. Moreover, recent violence against the indigenous peoples in Darfur has sent 300,000 people across the border to Chad, a reprise of the Darfur Refugee Crisis in the early 2000s. In these new and often inhospitable environments, the indigenous peoples lose their cultural and social spaces and face marginalization, extreme poverty, and human rights violations.
Objectives of the Project : The project aims to safeguard Sudanese intangible cultural heritage (ICH) and enhance community resilience, particularly among youth, despite ongoing conflict. Key outcomes include: 1. Assessment and documentation of at-risk ICH elements in seven localities (Port Sudan, Hadalia, Arbaat, Kassala, Gadareif, ElDamer, Dongola) in five states (Red Sea, Kassala, Gadareif, Northern Sudan and the River Nile). 2. Strengthening of professional and community capacities to protect ICH. The sub objectives of the project are: 1. Establishment of an expert assessment team to conducting assessments across targeted cities, 2. Organizing seven workshops to empower 140 youth (50% women) in ICH resilience. 3. Creating a community resilience training guidelines, conducting ICH assessments, and implementing youth-led cultural campaigns in local communities to preserve and promote cultural heritage.
